# Conclusions (revised analysis)

*Generated by `src/make_summary.py` from the files in `results/`. Do not edit numbers by hand: re-run the script.*

## One sentence

At equal citations, field and birth decade, women scientists' Wikipedia pages receive about 40% fewer links from other scientists' pages than men's (rate ratio 0.60, 95% CI [0.51, 0.70]), give fewer links themselves, and are more often cut off from the network altogether; their text is also recognisably different even with names and gender words hidden.

The claim is **less embedded**, not *less visible*: we measure links between scientists' pages, not readers.

## RQ1. Embeddedness at equal impact

Comparison set: 2,926 physicists and chemists matched to OpenAlex (606 women, 2,320 men), inside a network of 9,680 pages and 10,563 links.

**Raw numbers (not adjusted, for orientation only)**

| | Women | Men |
|---|---|---|
| Links received (mean in-degree) | 0.56 | 1.51 |
| Links given (mean out-degree) | 0.81 | 1.52 |
| Reciprocal links (mean) | 0.36 | 0.75 |
| No incoming link | 67.0% | 48.8% |
| No outgoing link | 56.1% | 42.1% |
| Isolate (no link in or out) | 51.5% | 33.7% |

**Against the null** (gender shuffled within strata, network fixed, 1,000 shuffles). Ratio = women's observed value / value expected under shuffling.

| Outcome | Field × decade × citation quintile | z | Subfield × decade × citation tercile | z |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Links received | 0.66 | -4.6 | 0.72 | -3.4 |
| Links given | 0.75 | -4.8 | 0.81 | -3.5 |
| Reciprocal links | 0.76 | -3.3 | 0.85 | -2.0 |
| Share with no incoming link | 1.10 | +3.8 | 1.04 | +1.6 |
| Share isolated | 1.20 | +5.3 | 1.10 | +3.2 |

The subfield strata are fine-grained: only 538 of 606 women sit in a stratum that also contains a man (against 596 for the coarser strata), so that test has less power. The gap in links received and given holds; the share with no incoming link is no longer distinguishable from the null there (z = +1.6).

**Count models for links received** (female coefficient as a rate ratio; controls: log citations, field, birth decade, deceased)

| Model | Women / men | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Negative binomial (headline) | 0.60 | [0.51, 0.70] |
| Poisson, robust SE | 0.58 | [0.49, 0.68] |
| Poisson, SE clustered by link community | 0.58 | [0.48, 0.70] |
| Hurdle, part 1: any incoming link (percentage points) | -9.2 | [-13.8, -4.6] |
| Hurdle, part 2: links, given at least one | 0.52 | [0.40, 0.69] |
| Prose-only links, negative binomial | 0.48 | [0.38, 0.59] |
| Links *given* (out-degree), negative binomial | 0.68 | [0.59, 0.78] |
| Supplement: PageRank, log scale (old headline) | 0.85 | [0.80, 0.91] |

The old headline ("14% lower PageRank") understated the gap. Almost half of the pages sit at the PageRank floor, so a log-PageRank ratio compresses a 40% gap in links into about 15%.

**What the gap runs through** (negative binomial, controls added one at a time)

| Specification | Women / men | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| baseline: citations, field, decade, deceased | 0.60 | [0.51, 0.70] |
| + subfield (OpenAlex) | 0.65 | [0.55, 0.76] |
| + page length (log words) | 0.62 | [0.53, 0.72] |
| + links on the page (log) | 0.71 | [0.61, 0.82] |
| + out-degree to scientists (log) | 0.81 | [0.72, 0.92] |
| + Nobel and awards | 0.58 | [0.50, 0.67] |

Page length does not account for the gap. The number of links on the page and the page's own links to scientists account for part of it. These are pathways, not confounders (linking is often mutual), so the honest reading is: women's pages are less woven into the network in both directions, and we cannot separate "others link to them less" from "their pages link out less".

**Field × gender in one model** (physics, chemistry and biology on the full three-field network, 12,463 pages, n = 3,866)

| Field | n (women) | Women / men | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Physics | 1,758 (349) | 0.59 | [0.47, 0.74] |
| Chemistry | 1,078 (240) | 0.69 | [0.54, 0.89] |
| Biology | 1,030 (344) | 0.64 | [0.47, 0.88] |

Joint test that the gap differs between fields: p = 0.66. On the count scale biology is **not** an exception; the earlier "biology gap almost disappears" came from the log-PageRank scale, where biology's larger share of unlinked pages hides the difference. What is different in biology is page length: women's pages are about 19% longer there (ratio 1.00 in physics).

**Robustness** (`results/rq1_robustness.csv`)

| Variant | n (women) | Links received: obs/expected (z) | NB rate ratio [95% CI] | Links given: obs/expected | Isolates: obs/expected |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Main: all wikilinks | 2,926 (606) | 0.66 (-4.7) | 0.60 [0.51, 0.70] | 0.75 | 1.20 |
| Prose-only links | 2,926 (606) | 0.55 (-4.5) | 0.48 [0.38, 0.59] | 0.78 | 1.15 |
| Subfield strata + subfield control | 2,926 (606) | 0.72 (-3.7) | 0.65 [0.55, 0.76] | 0.81 | 1.10 |
| Impact = h-index (largest profile) | 2,926 (606) | 0.65 (-4.9) | 0.57 [0.49, 0.68] | 0.73 | 1.21 |

## Selection check

Only pages with an ORCID or OpenAlex ID on Wikidata can be compared at equal citations. Match rates:

| Birth decade | Women matched | Men matched |
|---|---|---|
| 1920s | 2% of 177 | 1% of 1706 |
| 1930s | 6% of 170 | 10% of 1813 |
| 1940s | 23% of 238 | 30% of 1902 |
| 1950s | 49% of 317 | 50% of 1435 |
| 1960s | 64% of 287 | 62% of 934 |
| 1970s | 72% of 255 | 62% of 399 |
| 1980s | 75% of 20 | 60% of 20 |

Born 1970 or later: 33% of matched women and 11% of matched men (all pages: 19% and 5%).

Gap in links received **without** a citation control (field, decade, deceased, page length, prizes), by match status:

| Pages | n (women) | Raw mean in-degree, women / men | NB rate ratio | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all pages | 9,673 (1464) | 0.48 / 1.20 | 0.50 | [0.45, 0.55] |
| matched (comparison set) | 2,926 (606) | 0.56 / 1.51 | 0.51 | [0.44, 0.59] |
| not matched | 6,747 (858) | 0.42 / 1.08 | 0.50 | [0.43, 0.58] |

The gap among the 6,747 unmatched pages is the same size as among matched pages, so it is not created by the matching. Reweighting the comparison set to resemble all pages gives a rate ratio of 0.48 [0.38, 0.61] (unweighted Poisson 0.58). What this cannot show is whether the gap holds *at equal citations* among unmatched people: that needs `r4b_openalex_namematch.py`, which is written but **not run** (the OpenAlex API was not reachable from the machine used for the revision).

## RQ3. Who links to women's pages

154 of the 696 links to women's pages come from women's pages (22.1%); women's pages are 9.6% of all linking pages.

| Null (gender shuffled within…) | Expected share | z |
|---|---|---|
| field × decade (original) | 16.1% | +4.3 |
| link community, 10 Louvain partitions | 12.3% to 12.8% | +8.0 to +9.0 |
| link community × decade (revised), 10 Louvain partitions | 13.1% to 13.7% | +6.2 to +7.3 |
| link community × decade × field, 10 Louvain partitions | 12.9% to 13.9% | +6.5 to +7.7 |

The result does **not** disappear under the community × decade null: it gets stronger. The original null moved gender labels onto pages regardless of whether they link at all, which overstated how many links from women to expect. About 85% of linked women sit in a community × decade cell that also contains a man, so the null has room to move. The "to men" z-score of the old analysis is the same fact seen from the other side and is not reported as a second finding. The within-community PageRank percentile is dropped: it restated RQ1 without an impact control.

Women are 5.3% to 17.5% of the 16 link communities with at least 100 pages (one Louvain partition). They are present in every large community but unevenly; we do not claim they are spread evenly.

## RQ2. How the pages are written

**Classifier.** TF-IDF + logistic regression on the masked text, 5-fold cross-validated, 2,926 pages, 6,620 words.

| | Observed AUC | Shuffled-gender null (mean, 95% range) | z |
|---|---|---|---|
| All pages pooled | 0.859 | 0.576 [0.545, 0.605] | +16.8 |
| Within field × birth decade | 0.846 | 0.497 [0.456, 0.534] | +17.6 |

Field, birth decade, citations, page length and deceased alone give AUC 0.71. The pooled null sits at 0.58, not 0.50, because a classifier can learn cohort and field from text; the within-stratum AUC removes that and its null sits at 0.50. Dropping a further list of leak words changed the within-stratum AUC from 0.849 to 0.846.

**What an AUC this high does and does not mean.** It shows the pages differ systematically. It does not show that the difference is in how women are *described*. The strongest women-side words include British spellings and house-style verbs (*whilst, honours, characterisation, considers, earned, completed*), which would fit pages written recently by a small number of editors with a consistent style. We could not test this (it needs each page's creator and creation date from the revision history). Treat authorship as a live alternative explanation.

**Distinguishing words, within field × birth decade**

- Women's pages: education, career, earned, completed, recognition, interested, nomination, moved, earning, life, receive, early, aps, union, joined, doctorate, who, master
- Men's pages: under, quantum, received, born, theory, among, known, range, theoretical, field, visiting, papers, non, founding, index, approach, china, since

Of the 60 strongest words from the unadjusted comparison, 100% keep their direction inside birth decades and 92% stay beyond |z| = 1.96; the ones that do not: young, emeritus, called, nobel, shared. Words with |z| > 3: 166 unadjusted, 83 within field × decade (part of the drop is cohort, part is the smaller cells).

**Held-out check.** Words chosen on one random half of the pages point the same way in the other half 93% of the time (range 87% to 100% over 100 splits; chance is 50%), and 42% are also beyond |z| = 1.96 in the held-out half. Direction replicates; individual words should not be over-read.

**Explicit gender mentions** ("first woman to", "female physicist"; unmasked text): 15.5% of women's pages, 0.1% of men's; adjusted difference 16.6 points [13.5, 19.7].

**Dropped.** The personal-life word list (it found 51% of personal sentences on women's pages but 33% on men's, so it cannot compare genders), and with it the 4.9% vs 2.8% difference in the top citation quintile, which stays an untested lead.

## What is still open

1. **Human validation.** `validation/` holds blind sheets for two people (100 matches, 300 sentences). Until they are filled in, the only labels are AI-assisted, and the paper must say so. 50 of 50 correct per gender has a 95% interval of 93% to 100%: it cannot rule out a difference in match quality between women and men.
2. **Selection at equal citations.** Run `r4b_openalex_namematch.py` with the OpenAlex key.
3. **Page age and authorship.** Creation date and creator per page (one revisions API call each) would test the two main alternative explanations: women's pages are newer, and they are written by fewer editors.
4. **h-index** comes from the largest OpenAlex profile while citations are summed over split profiles; the single-profile row in the robustness table avoids the mismatch and gives the same answer.
